extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, legal scholars, policymakers, and researchers working on AI-related patent issues
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether AI-related inventions (particularly software and computer-implemented inventions) meet U.S. patent subject-matter eligibility and related judicial standards under 35 U.S.C. §101 and post-Alice case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter under 35 U.S.C. §101
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Section 101 of Title 35 of the United States Code, the scope of patentable subject matter is confined to any "new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof." This provision excludes claims that pertain to abstract concepts (such as mathematical formulas), naturally occurring phenomena, or fundamental scientific principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court has justified these exclusions because such ideas are the essential building blocks of scientific and technological progress and granting exclusive rights over them could obstruct innovation. Use this statutory baseline to determine whether an invention falls into one of the statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition) before considering judicial exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract idea / judicial exceptions (Alice-era constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that describe abstract concepts (e.g., mathematical algorithms or mental processes) or that are "capable of being executed by 'an ordinary mental process', 'within the human mind', or 'by an individual using pen and paper'" have been routinely treated as ineligible unless they demonstrate a distinct technological advancement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank, courts apply heightened scrutiny to software- and AI-related claims. If a claim merely recites an abstract idea or mental process (even if tied to a computer), it risks invalidation absent an 'inventive concept' that transforms the idea into patent-eligible subject matter. Examples of anti-patterns: framing routine human reasoning or basic data manipulation as a patentable computer-implemented invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of an 'inventive concept' / concrete technological improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: To survive Alice-era analysis, claims that might otherwise be characterized as abstract must exhibit an 'inventive concept'—a distinct technological advancement or concrete improvement in existing computer-related technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have invalidated AI-related patents that focus on predictive analytics or other algorithmic/mental processes when the claims lacked a concrete improvement to computer technology (e.g., Purepredictive, Inc. v. H2O.AI, Inc.). Conversely, a claim that meaningfully improves the functioning of a computer or other technological system is more likely to be patent-eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that merely apply an abstract idea using standard computer components are ineligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that implement an abstract idea by invoking a generic or conventional computer/system without adding a technical improvement are treated as attempts to monopolize the abstract idea and are thus ineligible (as in Blue Spike, LLC v. Google Inc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting or evaluating claims, avoid relying solely on conventional computer implementation language (e.g., 'using a computer', 'executed by a processor') as that will not supply the inventive concept required under Alice; instead, identify and claim the specific nonconventional technological feature or improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heightened difficulty patenting AI that replicates human cognitive functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Because AI systems often replicate cognitive functions typically performed by humans, they are particularly susceptible to characterization as abstract ideas under current §101 jurisprudence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that courts may analogize AI functionality to human mental processes, increasing the risk of ineligibility. Patent drafters should emphasize technical particulars, machine-centric improvements, or concrete system-level benefits to distinguish AI inventions from mere automation of human reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical impact of post-2014 jurisprudence on AI/software patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes introduced to criteria for patentable subject matter in 2014 (Alice decision) have made the path to patenting AI and software technologies significantly more rigorous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This heightened standard affects strategy: applicants and advisers must consider §101 risk early, craft claims that highlight technological solutions and improvements, and be prepared to address eligibility challenges. The article notes broader concerns about how these tightened standards may impede innovation and the need for careful legal and policy analysis.
